newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX down as market slows before holiday.
newsitem.headline: German DAX down as market slows before holiday.

text.p: German shares took a break from their recent turbulence on Wednesday as activity slowed ahead of Thursday's national holiday.
The blue chip DAX index eased to close the bourse session down 16.30 points at 3,551.98 points, with business firmly focused on companies at the centre of the day's news.
The index later ended post-bourse IBIS electronic dealings at 3,357.45, pressured by a sell-off on Wall Street.

Airline Deutsche Lufthansa rose after announcing a swing to first quarter profits while drugs group Bayer sank on news of a likely substantial payout to friends and relatives of AIDS sufferers infected by blood products.

"In many ways we can write off the week already. A lot of big investors will stay out of the market on Friday as well," said a Frankfurt trader. "Apart from Lufthansa and a few others, most of the moves appear to be almost accidental."
The Dow's 0.15 percent gain to a new record high was supporting but unconvincing, dealers said, while softer bond prices and the flagging dollar were sapping some energy.
Lufthansa bucked the trend to rise 85 pfennigs to 26.85 marks on significant volumes after news of a 20 million mark profit in the first quarter of 1997.
News of an 18.7 percent rise in first quarter operating profit also boosted Bayerische Vereinsbank, which ended up 1.80 marks at 74.80.

Bayer AG fell 2.28 marks, or 3.3 percent, to 67.25 marks on news a final settlement would soon be reached forcing it to pay some 460 million marks to friends and relatives of more than than 6,000 hemophiliacs infected with Aids through tainted blood products.
The group said after share trading had ended that it would pay $270 million as part of a broader $600 million settlement that included a total of four firms.

Dealers said the company was widely expected to have made adequate provision for this cost but that sentiment had also been marred by a slight earnings estimate cut on Bayer by a major German research house.
